title: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.
summary: An actress did not have to accept a different and inferior substitute role to reduce damages after the studio cancelled her promised musical role.
notes: The plaintiff was the actress Shirley MacLaine (Parker was her married name); the decision is 3 Cal.3d 176, 474 P.2d 689 (Cal. 1970), and Justice Sullivan's dissent argued that jobs must be of different kinds, not merely different, and that comparability was a fact question unsuited to summary judgment.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was actress Shirley MacLaine Parker. Twentieth Century-Fox was the studio that contracted for her performance and offered a substitute production after cancelling the original film.
sections.Material Facts: The studio promised Parker $750,000 in guaranteed compensation for fourteen weeks as the female lead in Bloomer Girl, a musical to be filmed in California. It abandoned the film and expressly notified her that it would not perform the agreement. It offered the leading role in Big Country, Big Man, a dramatic western to be filmed in Australia. The offered compensation was the same, and thirty-one of thirty-four numbered provisions matched. But the new role did not employ her musical and dancing talents in the same way, required a different location, and eliminated or impaired her original rights to approve the director and screenplay. She did not accept within the one-week period offered.
sections.Procedural History: The studio admitted the contract and its own breach but asserted a failure to mitigate. Parker obtained summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest. The California Supreme Court affirmed in 1970. Justice Sullivan dissented on whether the adequacy of the alternative could properly be resolved without trial.
sections.Issue: Could the studio deduct compensation Parker could have earned in the substitute film from the damages for cancellation of the original role?
sections.Holding: No. The substitute employment was different and inferior under the majority’s analysis, so Parker’s rejection did not reduce her recovery. There was no triable factual issue on the studio’s sole mitigation defense as the majority understood the record.
sections.Reasoning:
The employer bears the burden of establishing earnings actually obtained or reasonably available through comparable or substantially similar employment. An injured employee is not required to accept work of a different or inferior kind merely because it pays the same amount. The majority identified both differences in the work and an inferiority in the contractual rights: a dramatic western in Australia was different from a musical in California, and the loss of director and screenplay approvals reduced Parker’s control.

The court did not treat the monetary salary as the entire promised position. It also did not decide whether Parker made a reasonable general job search, because the studio had confined its defense to this specific substitute. Once the alternative was classified as different or inferior, rejecting it was not an avoidable-loss failure. Other arguments Parker made about her original contractual rights were unnecessary to reach.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Parker shows that mitigation protects an employee’s substantial nonmonetary interests as well as pay. Its procedural disagreement also warns against treating every difference between two jobs as automatically decisive.

topics.remedies: Protects guaranteed compensation when the proposed substitute is different or inferior.
topics.mitigation: Explains the employer’s burden and limits on requiring substitute employment.
topics.repudiation: Fox expressly notified Parker that it would not perform, which fixed the moment from which the avoidable-loss analysis ran.
topics.expectation-interest: The $750,000 award is the full expectation measure for a wrongfully discharged employee, reduced only by earnings from comparable employment.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Sullivan argued that differences between productions are inevitable and do not by themselves establish a different kind of employment. Their significance, the lost contractual rights, and countervailing benefits ordinarily require factual evaluation. He objected to deciding comparability as a matter of law on this record.
